new_statements.quote: Stress patterning is predictable, and is regulated by three factors: (a) All words contain stress groups consisting of two or three syllables, of which only the initial syllable carries stress; (b) Morpheme boundaries between roots of reduplicated and compound stems affect the patterning; (c) The initial syllable of a word carries primary stress.
new_statements.citation: Wood, Ray. 1978. Some Yuulngu phonological patterns. In: Papers in Australian Linguistics No. 11 (Pacific Linguistics A-51), 53-117. Canberra: Australian National University.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3.1 'Factors regulating stress patterning', p. 85 (p. 33 of the extracted file; p. 93 of the full PL A-51 scan); exceptions sec. 3.6 p. 87
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: opened (65 pp., text present) and the page scan. Book p. 85 (p. 33), sec. 3 'THE STRESS GROUP', 3.1 'FACTORS REGULATING STRESS PATTERNING', reads word for word: 'Stress patterning is predictable, and is regulated by three factors: (a) All words contain stress groups consisting of two or three syllables, of which only the initial syllable carries stress; (b) Morpheme boundaries between roots of reduplicated and compound stems affect the patterning; (c) The initial syllable of a word carries primary stress.' Secondary-stress and exception details (3.3-3.6, pp. 86-87: 'ss"ss / 'sss"ss / 'sss"sss groups; 'second and subsequent groups are subordinate'; five-syllable words always 3+2…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of every word; the word is parsed into two- or three-syllable stress groups from the left, each group-initial syllable carrying (weaker) secondary stress; a reduplication or compound boundary restarts the parse. Stated for the Gaalpu (Galpu) dialect and the Yuulngu (Yolngu) complex generally, not specifically for Dhay'yi.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Sec. 3.3-3.5 pp. 86-87: four-to-six-syllable words have two groups ('ss"ss, 'sss"ss, 'sss"sss); the second and later groups are 'subordinate', their initial syllable carrying weaker stress than the word-initial one; five-syllable words are always 3+2, never 2+3; in seven-syllable words secondary stress placement (third vs fourth syllable) is hard to hear.
new_statements.exceptions: Sec. 3.6 p. 87: 'Some words occur which appear to constitute exceptions to the normal patterns. They are mainly pronominals' (e.g. genitive-dative pronouns heard with initial stress only); also a few words with non-initial stress: pu.'ral.ku 'place name', pur.'wu 'flower', pur.'wu.mi 'in flower', pa.'dak ~ 'pa.dak 'still'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (stress group within the phonological word, including suffixed and nominalised forms); based on fieldwork at Galiwin'ku 1973-76 with Galpu-speaking informants. Not a Dhay'yi description: Wood's scope statement (sec. 0.1, p. 54) is 'the phonological patterns of a particular Yuulngu dialect, Gaalpu, and.. the phonology of the Yuulngu language complex generally'; Dha'yi (Dhalwangu, Djarrwark) appears only in his dialect classification (p. 57, fig. 1 p. 59).
new_statements.identity_note: Dayi = Dhay'yi (Glottolog dayi1244, ISO dax), the language of the Dhalwangu (Yirritja) and Djarrwark (Dhuwa) clans of north-east Arnhem Land; Wikipedia and Dixon subsume it under Dhuwal (dhuw1249). The quoted Wood 1978 statement is for the Gaalpu/Galpu communalect (a Dhangu variety; Glottolog galp1234 per Wood's fig. 1, not verified here) framed as general to the Yuulngu (Yolngu) complex; it is not a Dhay'yi description.

new_statements.quote: (p.278) The only systematically 'resistive' position within a word is the initial syllable, which is the stressed syllable in Yolngu languages. (p.xv) There are three vowels, and non-contrastive vowel length may occur in the primary-stressed syllable, which is usually the first syllable of a word. Djinang (like other Yolngu languages) has fewer constraints on consonant clusters than do many other Australian languages. (p.122) In most Yolngu languages, it appears to be -mara (e.g. Dhuwala/Dhuwal, Ritharrngu, Dhay?yi).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-initial stress across Yolngu languages (group-level claim).
new_statements.identity_note: group-level statement: Waters states that the initial syllable is the stressed syllable 'in Yolngu languages'; Dhay?yi is named (p.122) as one of the Yolngu languages compared, but no Dhay'yi-specific prosodic data are given. [name in source: Dhay?yi; pages p.122 (named among Yolngu languages sharing CAUS -mara); Yolngu-wide stress remarks p.xv and p.278] | Ritharngu (Glottolog rita1239 'Ritharrngu'), the southernmost Yuulngu language and Dhay'yi's south-western neighbour. Ch. 1 pp. 1-2 lists 'Dhuwal, Dhuwala, Dhay?yi, Dha:ngu, Dja:ngu, Nha:ngu' as the named Yuulngu languages and p. 7 gives a tentative subgrouping (Ritharngu | Dhuwal Dhuwala Dhuwaya Dhay?yi within southern Yuulngu); the phonology (ch. 2) is Ritharngu only. | Dayi (Dhay'yi: Dhalwangu, Djarrwark clan lects) is never named in the volume. The volume types Dhuwal (11) and Djapu (12, a Dhuwal clan lect) in figure 1 and calls the Yolngu languages 'strictly left oriented'; Glottolog puts Dayi and Dhuwal-Dhuwala together in Southern-Eastern Yolngu (sout3149), and Dhuwal/Dhuwala/Dhay'yi are commonly described as mutually intelligible varieties of one Yolngu Matha dialect chain. Other-variety glottocode dhuw1249. The searcher's note that no Southern-Eastern Yolngu lect appears in the volume is not right (Dhuwal and Djapu are in figure 1), but this is figure typing plus a family-level remark only. Pointer, low confidence. [name in source: Dhuwal (no. 11), Djapu (no. 12); 'Yolngu languages'; pages 66 (figure 1 key), 72, 77]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Incidental lexicographer's remark presupposing that Yolngu-Matha words carry accent on the first syllable as the regular case (hence no accent marking needed in dictionary lemmas), with a few lexical exceptions to be listed: marika (clan name) accented on the penult, muka (interrogative particle) on the final syllable, 'and so on'.
new_statements.exceptions: marika (clan name) with penultimate accent; muka (interrogative particle) with final accent; 'and so on' (an open list of lexical exceptions).
new_statements.identity_note: A planning paper for Zorc's pan-Yolngu-Matha dictionary (the 1986 dictionary already held by the project as silent). Its scope explicitly spans all Yolngu 'language types' incl. dhay'yimirr and lists Dhalwangu among the dialects coded (p. 34, (b)-(c)); the accent remark on p. 33 is made for Yolngu-Matha as a whole ('particularly the case in a pan-Yolngu-Matha dictionary'), not from Dhay'yi data. Same identity caveat as Wood 1978 / Waters 1989: a Yolngu-general statement, not a Dhay'yi description.
